source.title: FNBench: Benchmarking Robust Federated Learning against Noisy Labels
source.authors: Xue Jiang; Jia Li; Nannan Wu; Zhiyuan Wu; Xu-Jing Li; Sheng Sun; Gang Xu; Yuwei Wang; Qi Li; Min Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study measures test-accuracy curves during federated training and reports that the memorization warm-up pattern does not consistently hold when clients have varying noise rates.
record.gate_note: The study's own result on memorization is the test-accuracy pattern in Figure 5. Other memorization statements in the paper cite prior work and are not extracted as results.
record.test_reason: Figure 5 measures clean-test accuracy over federated training rounds, not when correctly labeled versus noisy examples are fitted. The presence or absence of a test-accuracy peak cannot establish V6's learning order. Other experiments measure noise robustness and representation quality without testing V1–V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases Section V-A: the authors interpret the inconsistent test-accuracy warm-up under heterogeneous client noise as showing that the memorization effect does not universally hold in FL. Their measurements establish variation in test-accuracy trajectories, but do not directly establish whether clean labels are learned before noisy labels.
record.recipe_differences: Federated learning with client-partitioned data and varying noise rates; measures test accuracy over training rounds rather than fitting fully random labels in centralized networks.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported pattern changes between the ideal setting with IID data and equal client noise rates and the more generalized settings with varying client noise rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Section V-A reports an early test-accuracy rise followed by decline for IID clients with equal noise rates, but no consistent warm-up for clients with varying noise rates under IID and Non-IID partitioning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The rise-then-decline pattern in federated clean-test accuracy depends on client data and label-noise heterogeneity.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing
record.problems: Figure 5 results are curves without numeric values in the supplied text. The paper does not directly measure separate learning of correct and noisy labels, and the tested federated CIFAR-10 settings do not test the claim's fully random-label condition.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on V6 were found. The paper's other reported experiments concern federated noisy-label robustness and representation regularization, not the behaviors named in these claim versions.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison between true and random labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases.
Perfect training fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit throughout a zero-to-complete corruption sweep and steadily increasing test error toward chance.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and generalization on true labels after removing them.
The temporal order of learning shared real-data patterns and memorizing noisy labels; no separate clean-example and noisy-example fitting trajectories are reported.

record.verdict_notes: The authors' interpretation alone does not make these test-accuracy curves a measurement of V6. No numerical Figure 5 values can be recovered from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test fitting completely random labels or report training error and test error at chance.
The study does not compare training time or convergence speed for random versus true labels.
The study does not train on shuffled pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.
The study does not sweep label corruption from none to all while measuring training and test error.
The study does not test whether explicit regularization or augmentation prevents fitting random labels or affects generalization on true labels.
The study measures test-accuracy curves under federated synthetic noisy-label conditions, but does not directly measure separate learning of real-label patterns and noisy or random labels.

rows.measure: Test accuracy over training rounds; text reports a warm-up pattern in which test accuracy increases early and then gradually decreases.
rows.note: The text says the warm-up pattern can basically be observed under the two ideal assumptions; the figure provides the curve.
rows.check: The reported early rise and subsequent decline in test accuracy is a generalization pattern, not a measurement of clean-label learning before noise memorization. The textual description is supported, but its V6 link and observed state are not.

rows.note: The paper says the effect does not consistently hold when clients have various noise rates. The text groups panels (b-c), so the separate curve values cannot be assigned to this condition.
rows.check: An absent test-accuracy warm-up does not establish absent clean-first learning. Section V-A reports the result collectively for Figure 5(b–c); individual curve values and the model or training method are not identified in the supplied figure text.

relation.reason: Section V-A discusses clean-first memorization and interprets test-accuracy trajectories through it, without measuring the learning order specified by V6.

tranche.reason: The reported test-accuracy trajectories and representation measurements do not establish training-set fitting or the relative learning order of clean and noisy labels. Under the related-construct exclusion, these results test none of V1–V6.

source_check.notes: The authors interpret inconsistent test-accuracy warm-up as evidence that memorization does not universally hold in FL; the measured trajectories cannot establish that conclusion about learning order. Figure 5 has no numerical curve values in the supplied text.
